newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek transport, industry hit by strikes.
newsitem.headline: Greek transport, industry hit by strikes.

text.p: Greek seamen ended a strike that had left hundreds of lorries stranded at ports with their loads of produce rotting, but transport was further hit on Thursday by a walkout by the nation's biggest labour group.
Seamen abandoned their 10-day strike, which had isolated Aegean islands, after the socialist government promised to discuss their demands for higher pensions, unemployment measures and lower taxes.
It was the first time the socialist goverment has shown signs of bending its tight economic policies in response to a series of strikes it won elections in September.
"We are not totally pleased with the deal but the government backed down on at least two demands," seamen's union representative Giorgos Maroulakis told Reuters.
Government spokesman Dimitris Reppas was quick to tell reporters the goverment's policy had not shifted.
"The seamen moved from their initial positions and the strike ended," Reppas said. "Our policy remains the same."
The Panhellenic Seamen's Federation (PNO) warned that it would repeat its walkout if talks with the government produced no results. The strike affected all ships with Greek crews.
Transport was also hit on Thursday by a nationwide strike called by Greece's biggest labour confederation, GSEE, against a new tax system, which abolishes most tax breaks.
Trains, urban buses and flights were disrupted, while GSEE claimed walkouts in construction, industry and textiles were a success, with participation reaching over 90 percent.
"We are pleased with the participation results and with the turnout at rallies around Greece," GSSE spokesman Giorgos Mavrikos told Reuters.
Airport officials said flights were re-scheduled around a three-hour work stoppage by employees of the national carrier Olympic Airways between 1000 and 1300 GMT, resulting in delays.
State hospitals, public services and several state companies operated with skeleton staff. High school teachers have been on an indefinite strike since Monday to push for better pay.

About 2,000 GSEE protesters marched through central Athens shouting slogans against the government and holding banners reading "Down with cuts in salaries and pensions" and "Down with the government's autocracy."

Prime Minister Costas Simitis drew up a strict 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, and announced tight new incomes and tax policies, saying the country needs bitter medicine to turn its ailing economy around.
His tough policies have raised a storm of reaction for a series of labour groups, including a paralysing road blockade by farmers in December, which Simitis successfully stared down.
Farmers have threatened to repeat their blockade if they get no government pledges by February 4 that their demands for higher price supports, fuel and tax cuts will be met.
